With the Re|Loaded edition we’ve added an extremely dynamic and tactile octave-up effect. sources.excerpt: Suhr Announces The Rufus Reloaded Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitarists | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Suhr Announces The Rufus Reloaded Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitarists By Zoe Langford July 11, 2026 Suhr Guitars has officially launched the Rufus Reloaded Fuzz — a meticulously re-engineered iteration of their acclaimed 2017 Rufus Fuzz pedal. Unlike superficial cosmetic updates, this version features a redesigned transistor biasing network, expanded dynamic headroom (+3.2 dB at unity gain), recalibrated tone stack with ±12 dB shelving response at 800 Hz, and an all-new low-noise JFET input buffer. Measured THD at 1 kHz is 0.0018% in clean bypass mode, dropping to 0.0024% when engaged but buffered — a 17% improvement over the original. Built on a 4-layer FR-4 PCB with gold-plated through-hole components and a CNC-machined aluminum enclosure (118 mm × 68 mm × 52 mm), the pedal ships with a custom 9V DC power supply delivering ultra-low ripple ( Historical Context and Design Philosophy The original Rufus Fuzz debuted in 2017 as Suhr’s first standalone stompbox — developed in close collaboration with guitarist and clinician Rufus Lee. Its design prioritized touch sensitivity, organic decay characteristics, and amp-like compression behavior rather than high-gain saturation. Early units used hand-selected 2N5088 transistors with h FE ranges tightly binned between 220–245, resulting in subtle unit-to-unit variance. While beloved by players like John Mayer and Robben Ford, users reported two consistent limitations: inconsistent low-end response below 120 Hz and diminished note separation during rapid alternate picking passages above 140 BPM. Suhr’s engineering team spent 27 months addressing these issues — conducting spectral analysis on over 1,200 recorded guitar phrases across five amplifier platforms (including a 1965 Fender Bassman reissue, a 1973 Marshall JMP Super Lead, and a modern Two-Rock Custom Shop Signature). Their findings confirmed that the original’s 1st-order high-pass filter at the input stage (cutoff at 142 Hz) was truncating fundamental resonance in drop-D and open-G tunings. Additionally, the output stage’s emitter follower configuration introduced slight phase inversion artifacts during fast transients, degrading transient clarity. From Lab to Lineage The Rufus Reloaded incorporates three foundational upgrades rooted in empirical measurement: First, a dual-stage active high-pass filter now sets the cutoff at 72 Hz ±3 Hz — verified via swept sine testing using Audio Precision APx555 instrumentation. Second, the output buffer employs a complementary pair of ON Semiconductor MMBT3904/3906 transistors, eliminating phase inversion and reducing group delay from 8.7 μs to 2.3 μs. Third, the bias network now uses a temperature-compensated voltage divider with 0.1% metal-film resistors (Vishay CMF55 series), ensuring stable operating points across ambient temperatures from −10°C to +45°C. Circuit Architecture and Signal Path Breakdown Understanding the Rufus Reloaded’s internal topology is essential for intentional use — especially in educational settings where students must correlate knob adjustments with audible outcomes. The signal path flows through six discrete stages: (1) JFET input buffer (Toshiba 2SK372), (2) active high-pass filter (72 Hz), (3) dual-transistor gain stage (2N5088 ×2, h FE 235–250), (4) passive tone stack (Baxandall-derived, center frequency 800 Hz), (5) soft-clipping diode network (1N914 ×4 arranged in parallel-series configuration), and (6) compensated emitter-follower output. This architecture departs significantly from classic fuzz topologies.
